choices.title: Bubble CPAP system
choices.correct_explanation:
•  Bubble continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) is a non-invasive ventilation system primarily used in neonates and infants to manage respiratory distress syndrome (RDS), apnea of prematurity, and other causes of respiratory insufficiency.

 Key Concepts

·      Structure: The system consists of:

  • A nasal interface (nasal prongs or mask)
  • A humidified gas source
  • A circuit where expiratory limb ends in a water chamber, allowing bubbles to form

·      Mechanism of action:

  • The bubbling creates oscillations that generate mild airway vibrations, aiding in gas exchange.
  • Positive pressure helps to keep alveoli open during expiration, improving functional residual capacity (FRC).
  • Reduces work of breathing and improves oxygenation and CO₂ elimination.

·      Pressure delivery:

  • The level of CPAP is determined by the depth of the expiratory tubing submerged in water (e.g., 5 cm below water = 5 cm H₂O pressure).

·      Advantages:

  • Simple and cost-effective
  • Does not require a ventilator
  • Promotes spontaneous breathing

Clinical Applications

·      Neonatal RDS

·      Meconium aspiration syndrome

·      Transient tachypnea of the newborn

·      Bronchopulmonary dysplasia (prevention)

Distractor option A: Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO)

Note:

·      ECMO is a highly invasive, extracorporeal life support technique used in severe cardiopulmonary failure.

·      It involves circulating blood outside the body through a machine that provides oxygen and removes CO₂, bypassing the lungs (veno-venous ECMO) or both heart and lungs (veno-arterial ECMO).

·      ECMO circuits include cannulas, membrane oxygenator, pump, and heat exchanger, which are visibly different from Bubble CPAP systems.

·      Used in cases like:

  • ARDS unresponsive to conventional ventilation
  • Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN)
  • Severe cardiac failure

Key concept: ECMO is a life-saving bridge, not a primary respiratory support modality.

 

Distractor option C: High-flow nasal cannula (HFNC)

Note:

·      HFNC delivers heated, humidified oxygen at high flows (up to 60 L/min in adults; ~8–12 L/min in neonates) via nasal cannula.

·      Provides a variable level of positive pressure, but not regulated or consistent like CPAP.

·      Does not use a water chamber to generate bubbling—a key distinguishing feature.

·      Used in:

  • Bronchiolitis
  • Mild to moderate respiratory distress
  • Post-extubation support

Key Differences

·      No bubbling chamber

·      No defined positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP)

·      Offers dead space washout, not pressure-driven alveolar recruitment.

Distractor option D: T-piece Resuscitator

Note:

·      T-piece resuscitators are used in neonatal resuscitation.

·      Delivers controlled positive pressure ventilation (PPV) and positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) using a manual operator-controlled system.

·      Commonly seen during resuscitation at birth, not for long-term oxygen delivery.

·      Components:

  • T-piece circuit with PEEP valve
  • Gas source
  • Mask or endotracheal tube interface

Key Distinction

·      Used for short-duration resuscitation, not ongoing respiratory support like bubble CPAP.

choices.title: 120–150 mmHg
choices.correct_explanation:
Endotracheal Suctioning: Clinical Importance

Endotracheal suctioning is performed to maintain airway patency, facilitate gas exchange, and prevent complications such as:

·      Hypoxemia

·      Atelectasis

·      Nosocomial infections (e.g., Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia)

        In critically ill patients, especially those on mechanical ventilation, ineffective secretion clearance can rapidly worsen oxygenation and ventilation status.

Role of Suction Pressure

The application of negative pressure is essential for mobilizing and removing secretions through the endotracheal tube. However, this must be balanced carefully:

·      Too low pressure: Ineffective secretion removal.

·      Too high pressure: Mucosal trauma, hypoxia, bronchospasm, atelectasis.

        Thus, selecting the correct suction pressure is a fundamental clinical skill.

Recommended Suction Pressures

Population

Suction Pressure (mmHg)

Neonates

60–80 mmHg

Children

100–120 mmHg

Adults

100–150 mmHg

These values are endorsed by:

·      American association for respiratory care (AARC)

·      European respiratory society (ERS)

·      Critical Care Societies

·      As per latest AIIMS guideline

Why is 120-150 mmHg Optimal for Adults?

·      Adults typically have larger airways and produce thicker, more viscous secretions.

·      A suction pressure of 120-150 mmHg provides:

  • Adequate negative force to mobilize secretions.
  • Minimal risk of mucosal trauma when performed with correct technique (pre-oxygenation, short duration <15 sec).

·      Suction pressures above this range significantly increase the risk of airway complications.

Distractors:

Option a: 60–80 mmHg

·      This is the recommended suction pressure for neonates.

·      Applying this to adults would be insufficient to clear secretions.

·      Clinical consequence: retained secretions → airway obstruction, hypoxia, atelectasis, increased work of breathing.

Option b. 80–120 mmHg

·      Appropriate for children (pediatric patients).

·      In adults, especially those critically ill or with copious secretions, this would often be inadequate.

·      Leads to ineffective suctioning, resulting in secretion stasis, promoting infection and respiratory compromise.

Option d: 150-200 mmHg

·      Excessively high suction pressure > 150 mmHg.

·      Clinical risks include:

  • The suction pressure > 150 mmHg will lead to trauma to tracheobronchial mucosa (ulceration, bleeding)
  • Bronchospasm due to irritation
  • Hypoxia from prolonged negative pressure exposure
  • Atelectasis due to alveolar collapse from excessive suction force.

·      This level is not recommended for any age group.

Clinical Relevance in ICU & Emergency

·      In ICU and emergency settings, improper suctioning technique, especially incorrect pressure, can rapidly deteriorate patient status.

·      Nurses must always verify suction pressure before the procedure.

·      Maintaining evidence-based suction pressure is part of standard infection control protocols and safe mechanical ventilation practices.

choices.correct_explanation:
PDPH- Post-Dural Puncture Headache
  • Post-dural puncture headache (PDPH) is a common post-procedure symptom. It occurs due to loss of CSF through the dura which causes traction on the pain-sensitive intracranial structures. The headache in PDPH is typically frontal or occipital.
  • May follow lumbar puncture, spinal anesthesia, wet epidural tap (in which epidural needle pierced dura).
  • Onset 12-72 hrs and last for 1-2 weeks.
  • It is aggravated with the upright or sitting posture and is relieved by lying supine.
  • Incidence increases with the larger needle, cutting point (in comparison to pencil point) needle, young age, females, pregnancy.
  • Prevention by thinner needle.Factors that can increase the incidence of headache after spinal puncture:
  • Age: younger, more frequent
  • Sex: Females > males
  • Needle size: Larger > smaller
  • Needle bevel: Less when the needle bevel is placed in the long axis of the neuraxis. Orienting a needle bevel parallel with the axis of the spine, such that the longitudinal fibers of the dura would more likely be separated than cut, results in a lower incidence of post spinal puncture headache.
  • Pregnancy: More when pregnant.
  • Dural punctures: More with multiple punctures.Factors that do not increase the incidence of headache after spinal puncture:
  • Insertion and use of catheters for continuous spinal anesthesia
  • Timing of ambulationManagement:
  • Supine position
  • IV fluids
  • Caffeine and analgesia
  • Epidural blood patch

Elbow restraints (also called No-No restraints) are commonly used in infants after cleft lip surgery to prevent the child from bending their arms and touching or injuring the surgical site on the face.

Other options:

  • Option-a: Jacket restraint: Used to restrict torso movement, often in cases like head/neck procedures or to prevent falling from a chair/crib—not specific to facial surgery.
  • Option-c: Mitten restraint: Prevents a child from scratching or pulling at devices/tubes but does not restrict elbow movement, so the child could still touch the lip.
  • Option-d: Wrist restraint: Usually applied in older children or adults to prevent pulling IV lines or catheters; not commonly used post cleft lip repair in infants.

choices.title: Vitamin D deficiency
choices.correct_explanation:
The above image shows bowing of legs along with frontal bossing are clinical features of rickets. Vitamin D deficiency is the most common cause of nutritional rickets.

·         Craniotabes (soft skull), frontal bossing, stunted growth, and craniosynostosis are clinical features of rickets.

·         General features include failure to thrive, listlessness, protruding abdomen, proximal muscle weakness, and fracture.

Head to toe-examination would include the following features:

·         Head examination would include craniotabes, frontal bossing, delayed fontanel closure, delayed dentition, and craniosynostosis.

·         Chest examination would reveal rachitic rosary, Harrison's sulcus, and repeated respiratory infections and atelectasis.

·         Spinal deformities could include kyphosis, scoliosis, lordosis.

·         Limb examination and extremities may show windswept deformity, anterior bowing of tibia, coxa vara, and enlargement of wrists and ankles. Bowings of legs (genu varum) or knock knees (genu valgum) may be noted. These changes can be seen only in children of the weight-bearing age group/ toddlers.

The image shows frontal bossing:

The image shows the rachitic rosary:

10 important clinical features in Rickets

Radiological features of rickets:

·         Loss of provisional zone of calcification: earliest radiological finding of rickets.

·         Delayed appearance of the epiphysis

·         Widening of growth plate: normal width of growth plate is 2-4mm. It is increased in cases of rickets due to excessive accumulation of uncalcified osteoid at the growth plate.

·         Cupping of metaphysis: normally metaphysis meets epiphysis as a smooth line of sclerosis. But in rickets the line is absent and the metaphyseal ends appear irregular and the cartilage accumulating in the growth plate creates a depression in the metaphysis causing cupping.

·         Fraying: indistinct margins of the metaphysis

·         Bowing of diaphysis, with thinning of cortices

·         In healing rickets, zone of calcification becomes denser.

Other options:

·        Option a: Vitamin A deficiency causes Night blindness.

·        Option b: Vitamin C deficiency causes Scurvy.

·        Option c: Vitamin K deficiency in neonates can cause Hemorrhagic disease of the newborn and in children may cause bleeding disorders.

Ayushman Bharat - Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (PM-JAY)

Ayushman Bharat-National Health Protection Mission (AB-NHPM) aims to build a comprehensive need-based health care service and targets to build a 'New India 2022'. Its components are: 

·       Creation of 1,50,000 Health and Wellness Centres: These centres will provide Comprehensive Primary Health Care (CPHC), covering both maternal and child health services and non-communicable diseases, including free essential drugs and diagnostic services.     

·       National Health Protection Mission (NHPM) provides health protection cover to poor and vulnerable families, screening for non-communicable diseases, and follow-up of hospitalization cases among others.

Ayushman Bharat - Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (PM-JAY), all pre-existing diseases are also covered. Hospitals cannot deny treatment.

Ayushman Bharat - Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (PM-JAY), the largest health assurance scheme in the world which aims at providing a health cover of Rs. 5 lakhs per family per year for secondary and tertiary care across public and private empaneled hospitals in India, to over 12 crores poor and vulnerable families

 

Benefits under the scheme:

·       The government provides health insurance coverage of up to Rs. 5,00,000 per family per year (Option B).

·       All families listed in the Socio-Economic Caste Census (SECC) database as per the defined criteria will be covered. No cap on family size and age of members

·       Priority is given to a girl child, women, and senior citizens.

·       Free treatment is available at all public and empaneled private hospitals in times of need.   

·       It covers secondary and tertiary care hospitalization.

·       1,929 procedures covering surgery, medical and daycare treatments, the cost of medicines, and diagnostics.

·       It covers up to 3 days of pre-hospitalization and 15 days of post-hospitalization expenses such as diagnostics and medicines.

·       All pre-existing diseases are covered. Hospitals cannot deny treatment.

·       Cashless and paperless access to quality health care services.

·       Hospitals will not be allowed to charge any additional money from beneficiaries for the treatment.  

·       A 24X7 helpline number is available for information, assistance, complaints, and grievances.

choices.title: Exposure
choices.correct_explanation:
• Exposure is the contact of a person with an environmental factor (physical, chemical, biological, or social) that may affect health.
  • These environmental factors may include:
    • Biological: Bacteria, viruses, fungi
    • Chemical: Pesticides, lead, pollutants
    • Physical: Radiation, noise, heat, cold
    • Environmental: Contaminated air, water, food, or soil
    • Exposure does not necessarily cause disease, but it provides the opportunity for a harmful agent to affect health.
    • Contact with an environmental agent that may influence health.
    • May or may not result in disease.
  • Examples:
    • Inhaling polluted air
    • Drinking contaminated water
    • Contact with an infected person
    • Exposure to radiation

B. Susceptibility

  • Refers to the likelihood or predisposition of an individual to develop disease after exposure.
  • It is a host factor, not the contact itself.

Example: An unvaccinated person is more susceptible to measles.

C. Invasion

  • Refers to the entry and spread of a pathogen into host tissues after exposure and colonization.
  • It is a stage in the infectious disease process.

Sequence: Exposure → Colonization → Invasion → Disease

D. Colonization

  • Refers to the presence and multiplication of microorganisms on body surfaces without causing disease.
  • The organism is present but has not invaded tissues.

Example: Nasal carriage of Staphylococcus aureus.

  • Free treatment is available at all public and empaneled private hospitals in times of need.
  • It covers secondary and tertiary care hospitalization.
  • 1,929 procedures covering surgery, medical and daycare treatments, the cost of medicines, and diagnostics.
  • It covers up to 3 days of pre-hospitalization and 15 days of post-hospitalization expenses such as diagnostics and medicines.
  • All pre-existing diseases are covered. Hospitals cannot deny treatment.
  • Cashless and paperless access to quality health care services.
  • Hospitals will not be allowed to charge any additional money from beneficiaries for the treatment.
  • A 24X7 helpline number is available for information, assistance, complaints, and grievances

choices.title: Index case
choices.correct_explanation:
• Index case is the first case that comes to the notice of an investigator or physician.
  • The primary case is the first case of a communicable disease introduced into a population unit.
  • A secondary case is one that develops after contact with the primary case.
  • A suspect case refers to a patient who has all the features of the disease but has not been diagnosed with it yet
  • Note: There is no such term as tertiary case

data.title: The first documented patient in a disease epidemic within a population is called:

choices.title: Cardiovascular disease
choices.correct_explanation:
• Cardiovascular diseases account for most NCD (Non-communicable diseases) deaths, or over 19 million people annually, followed by cancers (10 million), chronic respiratory diseases (around 4 million), and diabetes (1.6 million). Thus, option c. is correct.

 

National Programme for Prevention and Control of Cancer, Diabetes, Cardiovascular Disease, and Stroke

 

  • National Programme for Prevention and Control of Non-Communicable Diseases (NP-NCD), which was earlier called the National Programme for Prevention and Control of Cancer, Diabetes, Cardiovascular Disease, and Stroke (NPCDCS).
  • NPCDCS was launched in 2010 in order to prevent and control major NCD (non-communicable diseases). It focuses on strengthening infrastructure, human resource development, health promotion, early diagnosis, management, and referral.
  • Under NPCDCS, NCD Clinics are being set up at District and CHC levels, to provide services for early diagnosis, treatment, and follow-up for common NCD. NPCDCS has specialized facilities at the district hospital level. At the subcentre level under NPCDCS, screening and referral are done.
  • The NPCDCS has separate components for cancer and other non-communicable diseases like diabetes, and stroke. It has been implemented in over 100 districts in 21 states. For the cancer component, there is the Tertiary Care Cancer Centers (TCCC) scheme, which aims at setting up/strengthening State Cancer Institutes (SCI) and TCCCs all over the country, for providing comprehensive cancer care in the country

The new disease included in the NP-NCD:

  • Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD)
  • Chronic kidney disease
  • Asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
  • ST elevation myocardial infraction

choices.title: Meeting the enhanced nutritional needs of pregnant women and lactating mothers
choices.correct_explanation:
Pradhan Mantri Matru Vandana Yojana

  • Pradhan Mantri Matru Vandana Yojana (PMMVY) is a maternity benefit programme being implemented in all districts of the country with effect from 1st January, 2017.
  • It is a centrally sponsored scheme being executed by the Ministry of Women and Child Development.
  • Direct Benefit Transfer Scheme: Cash benefits are provided to pregnant women in their bank account directly to meet enhanced nutritional needs and partially compensate for wage loss. Thus, option a. is correct.
  • Target beneficiaries:
    • All Pregnant Women and Lactating Mothers (PW and LM), excluding those who are in regular employment with the Central Government or the State Governments or PSUs or those who are in receipt of similar benefits under any law for the time being in force.
    • All eligible pregnant women and lactating mothers who have their pregnancy on or after 1st January 2017 for the first child in the family.
  • Benefits under the scheme:
    • Beneficiaries receive a cash benefit of Rs.5,000 in three installments on fulfilling the following conditions:
      • Early registration of pregnancy.
      • Ante-natal check-up.
      • Registration of the birth of the child and completion of first cycle of vaccination for the first living child of the family.
      • The eligible beneficiaries also receive cash incentive under Janani Suraksha Yojana (JSY). Thus, on an average, a woman gets Rs. 6,000.
